title: UROFACIAL SYNDROME 1
alt_titles: FACIAL PALSY, PARTIAL, WITH URINARY ABNORMALITIES
INVERTED SMILE AND OCCULT NEUROPATHIC BLADDER

intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that urofacial syndrome-1 (UFS1) is caused by homozygous mutation in the HPSE2 gene on chromosome 10q24.

checks.claim: Urofacial syndrome-1 (UFS1) is caused by homozygous mutation in the HPSE2 gene.
checks.evidence_quote: Homozygous exonic deletions, nonsense mutations, and frameshift mutations in five further unrelated families confirmed HPSE2 as the causative gene for UFS.
checks.explanation: Abstract states homozygous HPSE2 mutations cause UFS.

checks.claim: The HPSE2 gene is located on chromosome 10q24.
checks.evidence_quote: Previously, we localized the defective gene for the urofacial syndrome (UFS) to a region on chromosome 10q24 by homozygosity mapping. We now report evidence that Heparanse 2 (HPSE2) is the culprit gene for the syndrome.
checks.explanation: The gene for the syndrome maps to 10q24, and HPSE2 is identified as that gene.

paragraphs.text: Urofacial syndrome (UFS) is a rare autosomal recessive disorder. Its main features are an 'inverted' facial expression, in which patients look as if they are crying when they smile, and a neurogenic bladder that does not empty completely even though there is no anatomic outflow obstruction or overt neurologic damage. Patients have enuresis, urinary tract infection, hydronephrosis, and vesicoureteral reflux. This can lead to kidney damage, and some severely affected patients develop hypertension and end-stage renal disease (Wang et al., 1997; Derbent et al., 2009; Daly et al., 2010).

paragraphs.text: Elejalde (1979) reported 7 patients (4 females and 3 males) from unrelated families. One family was consanguineous (first cousins). The patients had peculiar facies and gestures when smiling and crying. Their urinary findings included hydronephrosis, hydroureter, intravesical stenosis of the ureter, abnormal caliber of the prostatic and membranous urethra, and urethral valves. The bladder was abnormal, with trabeculation and diverticula, and the mucosa showed severe hypertrophy with sclerotic changes. Elejalde (1979) noted that the peculiar facies allows the condition to be recognized early.

paragraphs.text: Between 1965 and 1986, Ochoa and Gorlin (1987) saw 36 children with enuresis and urinary tract infection together with an 'inversion' of facial expression when laughing. Urologic workup showed mild neuropathic bladder in all cases, and most patients had severe urinary tract damage. About two-thirds of the patients also had moderate to severe constipation.

paragraphs.text: From a genetic analysis of 3 families, Elejalde (1979) concluded that the condition was probably autosomal dominant, with variable expressivity and incomplete penetrance. Ochoa and Gorlin (1987), however, concluded that the disorder is autosomal recessive. They based this on its occurrence in multiple sibs, normal parents, increased parental consanguinity, and an equal sex ratio. Homozygous HPSE2 mutations in affected individuals (Pang et al., 2010; Daly et al., 2010) confirmed autosomal recessive inheritance.

checks.claim: From a genetic analysis of 3 families, Elejalde (1979) concluded that the Ochoa syndrome was probably autosomal dominant with variable expressivity and incomplete penetrance.
checks.evidence_quote: The genetic analysis of these families indicates that the condition is probably autosomal dominant, with variable expressivity and incomplete penetrance.
checks.explanation: The title confirms there were three families. The conclusion matches.

checks.evidence_quote: The occurrence of the disorder in multiple sibs, normal parents, increased parental consanguinity, and equal sex ratio indicate autosomal recessive inheritance.
checks.explanation: The abstract lists the same four lines of evidence.

checks.claim: Homozygous HPSE2 mutations were found in individuals affected with urofacial syndrome.
checks.evidence_quote: Homozygous exonic deletions, nonsense mutations, and frameshift mutations in five further unrelated families confirmed HPSE2 as the causative gene for UFS.

checks.claim: Homozygous HPSE2 mutations in affected individuals confirmed autosomal recessive inheritance of urofacial syndrome.

checks.explanation: The title calls UFS autosomal recessive, and the gene was mapped by homozygosity mapping. The abstract does not explicitly say that homozygous mutations confirmed recessive inheritance.

paragraphs.text: Wang et al. (1997) performed a genome screen in 20 selected patients, combining homozygosity mapping with DNA pooling. The marker D10S677 showed an excess of homozygosity in patients compared with unaffected relatives (P less than 10(-6)). All 31 patients were homozygous for 2 closely linked markers, D10S1726 and D10S198, which lie about 5 cM telomeric to D10S677. Only 12% of unaffected relatives were homozygous for both markers (P less than 10(-19)). Recombination events placed the UFS gene within a 1-cM interval between D10S1433 and D10S603 on chromosome 10q23-q24.

paragraphs.text: Wang et al. (1999) confirmed linkage to the region identified by Wang et al. (1997) by homozygosity mapping in American patients of Irish heritage. Using new polymorphic markers, they narrowed the UFS gene to within a single YAC clone of 1,410 kb. Mutation analysis excluded the GOT1 gene, which lies in the critical region.

checks.explanation: The abstract refers back to the authors' earlier mapping of the same region and shows linkage to it in a new population. It does not name the 1997 paper, but 'previously, we' points to the authors' own prior work.

paragraphs.text: Chauve et al. (2000) carried out haplotype analysis in a French family. The results were compatible with the same critical region on 10q23-q24.

paragraphs.text: Wang et al. (2003) built a genomic sequence map of the UFS interval and narrowed the disease region to 220 kb. This region contains the ACDP1 gene and part of GOT1. Searches of the ACDP1 coding region, 5-prime and 3-prime untranslated regions, promoter, and exon/intron junctions found no pathogenic mutation in UFS patients.

checks.claim: The 220-kb urofacial syndrome region defined by Wang et al. (2003) contains the ACDP1 gene and part of GOT1.

checks.claim: Wang et al. (2003) found no pathogenic mutation in urofacial syndrome patients in the ACDP1 coding region, 5-prime and 3-prime untranslated regions, promoter, or exon/intron junctions.
checks.evidence_quote: Extensive search for mutations in the coding region, the 5' and 3' untranslated regions, the promoter region, and the exon/intron junctions failed to identify a pathogenic mutation in UFS patients.
checks.explanation: The abstract lists the regions searched and the negative result, but it does not say which gene was searched. ACDP1 is implied by context (GOT1 had already been excluded), but the abstract never names it.

paragraphs.text: Several studies concluded that UFS is genetically homogeneous. Wang et al. (1999) and Chauve et al. (2000) found linkage to the same region in American patients of Irish heritage and in a French family. Wang et al. (2003) concluded that the same gene on chromosome 10q is responsible for all UFS patients from multiple ethnic groups. In contrast, Daly et al. (2010) found no HPSE2 mutations in 4 UFS patients, which they interpreted as evidence of genetic heterogeneity.

checks.claim: Several studies concluded that urofacial syndrome is genetically homogeneous.
checks.evidence_quote: Here we demonstrate genetic homogeneity of the syndrome through homozygosity mapping in American patients with Irish heritage.
checks.explanation: This paper is one of the studies that concluded UFS is genetically homogeneous. The word 'several' relies on the other papers cited alongside it.

checks.claim: Wang et al. (1999) found linkage of urofacial syndrome to the same chromosome 10q region in American patients of Irish heritage.

checks.explanation: Showing homogeneity in American patients of Irish heritage means linkage to the same 10q region.

checks.evidence_quote: Haplotype analyses in our French family were compared with those previously described in patients from Columbia and America (literature data). The results are compatible with the same localization of the critical region
checks.explanation: The abstract describes haplotype analysis whose results were 'compatible with' the same region. It does not report a formal linkage finding, so 'found linkage' overstates it.

paragraphs.text: Pang et al. (2010) identified loss-of-function mutations in the HPSE2 gene in all UFS patients from Colombia, the United States, and France. These patients had previously been used to map the disorder to chromosome 10q24 by homozygosity mapping.

paragraphs.text: Daly et al. (2010) performed whole-genome SNP mapping in 1 individual with UFS and found a 16-Mb autozygous region on chromosome 10q23-q24. Within this region they identified a 10-kb deletion that removes exons 8 and 9 of HPSE2. In 5 further unrelated families, they found homozygous exonic deletions, nonsense mutations, and frameshift mutations in HPSE2. HPSE2 was expressed in the fetal and adult central nervous system and in bladder smooth muscle.

checks.claim: In 5 further unrelated urofacial syndrome families, Daly et al. (2010) found homozygous exonic deletions, nonsense mutations, and frameshift mutations in HPSE2.
checks.evidence_quote: Homozygous exonic deletions, nonsense mutations, and frameshift mutations in five further unrelated families confirmed HPSE2 as the causative gene for UFS.

checks.claim: Daly et al. (2010) found HPSE2 expressed in the fetal and adult central nervous system.
